transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-05-21
Time: 14:00 PT
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (AE), Priya (SE), Marcus (SRE) - Redwood; Samantha, Liam, Devin, Rajiv, Ana - BrightHealth AI
Links shared: Benchmark spreadsheet (shortlink: bit.ly/bhai-redwood-bench), SOC2 deck (drive link), demo recording from last week (drive link)

Summary Section (auto-generated, may be fuzzy):
- Reviewed Redwood vs baseline provider latency and throughput numbers, observed improvement on p50 but comparable p95 when network variance included. Discussed kv-cache and batching tuning. Agreed on follow-ups.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: All right everyone, thanks for joining. Quick agenda, we'll walk through the benchmark sheet, clarifying methodology, then dig into the p95 hotspots. Priya will walk the tuning steps we ran.
[00:18] Samantha: Sounds good, thanks. We are particularly interested in tail latency since our user flows are token-heavy, so p95 matters more than p50.
[00:29] Priya: Yep understood. Quick note on methodology: we ran three runs for each scenario, warm cache where applicable, 100 concurrent streams for hosted tests and dedicated runs at 16 GPUs with a target batch window of 20ms. Baseline provider numbers are what you gave us last week.
[00:47] Devin: Quick Q — when you say "warm cache" is that per-request KV or prefix cache?
[00:54] Priya: It's KV cache warm, we populated the kv cache with typical session prefixes to model chat workloads. There is some noise in the baseline because their tests were cold-start heavy.
[01:06] Liam: Baseline provider we run in prod has a 300ms p95 on 1k tokens, curious if that aligns with your number.
[01:15] Marcus: On Redwood dedicated with quantized model Q4 (int8-quant) we saw p50 ~85ms and p95 ~290ms for 1k-token prompt with kv-cache warm. That compares to baseline 300ms p95, so small win but similar tail.
[01:34] Samantha: Where did the 85ms p50 come from — that's impressive. Is that measured from client to token emitted or just server-side?
[01:41] Priya: Server-side emit time. End-to-end includes network, so add ~20-30ms typical for your region. Also note the p95 is sensitive to batching size and the model's attention length.
[01:55] Rajiv: From security perspective, were these runs on a private VPC or hosted? We need to understand egress controls.
[02:02] Jordan: These were hosted POC runs on Redwood's shared hosted cluster but isolated tenant buckets. For production you can choose Dedicated or Private VPC; we included a Dedicated run in the sheet to show that tail improved slightly when we pinned capacity.
[02:17] Ana: Any differences in tokenization between Redwood runtime and baseline that could skew tokens/sec?
[02:24] Priya: We used the same tokenizer model you provided; small tokenization diffs can happen due to preprocessing but we normalized the inputs. Throughput numbers reported are tokens/sec measured at server emit.
[02:38] [03:00] Jordan: Let's walk table by table — open the sheet, sheet tab A: baseline single-GPU hosted numbers, tab B: Redwood hosted, tab C: Redwood dedicated.
[03:15] Priya: For 512-token prompts, baseline p95 was ~160ms, our hosted p95 ~140ms. For 1k tokens baseline 300ms, our hosted 290ms, dedicated 260ms. Tokens/sec throughput: baseline 1.9k tokens/sec, Redwood dedicated 2.3k tokens/sec under same concurrency.
[03:42] Devin: Are those numbers with kv-cache enabled?
[03:45] Priya: The 1k results I quoted are with kv-cache warm. We also ran cold runs — those look worse, baseline suffers more on cold starts.
[03:58] Liam: What about batching? What's your max_batch_size used?
[04:03] Marcus: We set max_batch_size at 64 for hosted tests, and 128 on dedicated. But we also applied dynamic batching with a 20ms window which reduces per-token cost while keeping latency SLO.
[04:14] Samantha: I saw a note about quantization impacting quality, were you able to check delta on perplexity or eval set?
[04:20] Priya: We ran head-to-head on your eval prompts — BLEU-like style scoring is within 0.5% for int8 quant vs fp16 for most prompts, with a few edge-cases in long-range coherence. We flagged those in tab D.
[04:36] Rajiv: KMS + encryption question — when you ran dedicated, where were keys held?
[04:40] Jordan: For the Dedicated POC we used Redwood-managed KMS but can switch to customer-managed keys (CMK) in your AWS account for Private deployments. We'll attach the KMS integration doc.
[04:52] Ana: There's a row showing p95 spike at run #2 for one of your hosted tests — what happened there?
[04:57] Priya: That was a network jitter event on our infra at that time; we annotated the sheet with logs. When we excluded that outlier the p95 for hosted moves down about 15ms.
[05:09] Liam: Curious about GPU utilization — are you packing more streams per GPU which would explain higher tokens/sec?
[05:15] Marcus: Yes, on dedicated we tuned the scheduler to improve throughput — higher concurrency and longer max sequence means better utilization. We included util% column in the sheet; dedicated runs were about 78% GPU util versus baseline 64%.
[05:29] Samantha: Would constant higher util cause noisier tail latency?
[05:32] Priya: It can, especially if you oversubscribe. That's why we suggest conservative autoscaling and a small headroom margin for tail-sensitive workloads.
[05:41] Devin: Any notes on cost delta? If we push to dedicated to get p95 gains, what's the unit cost change?
[05:49] Jordan: We included an estimated $/1M tokens run-rate for both hosted and dedicated at typical utilization. Dedicated reduces $/token by ~18% at committed utilization but requires a reserve commit. We'll send the pricing scenarios.
[06:04] Rajiv: For compliance, can you provide audit logs for the POC activity?
[06:09] Jordan: Yes, we can export audit logs. I'll add a link to the SOC2 plus sample audit logs in the folder.
[06:17] Priya: Back to tuning — we tested enabling kv-cache on the client session vs server-managed prefix cache. Server-managed produced slightly better hit rates for chat-style sessions. That improved tokens/sec by ~10%
[06:33] Liam: Would enabling the kv-cache change cold-start behavior for new sessions?
[06:36] Priya: Cold starts still pay the penalty for absent cache, but for ongoing sessions hit rates go up quickly. We showed warm session curves in the sheet.
[06:45] Jordan: Ok let's dig into the p95 distribution graph on tab E — you can see our dedicated curve tighter in the right tail versus baseline.
[06:55] Samantha: One ask — can you rerun the 1k token test with kv-cache on but with network emulated to 100ms RTT to match our EU users?
[07:03] Priya: Yeah we can run an emulated RTT test. To be efficient, we'll do two seeds with 100ms RTT and include both hosted and dedicated. That will surface end-to-end numbers.
[07:13] Devin: Also include a run where you disable quantization so we can see worst-case latency and quality tradeoffs.
[07:19] Priya: Noted — will include fp16 baseline for that test.
[07:23] [07:50] Jordan: Anything else on methodology before we assign actions?
[07:33] Samantha: No that's it.
[07:36] Jordan: Great. Quick recap of the main findings: Redwood dedicated shows measurable throughput gains (2.3k vs 1.9k tokens/sec) and modest p95 improvements when pinned capacity; hosted has slightly better p50 and comparable p95 except for network noise. KV cache yields 10% throughput gain and tail improves for warm sessions. Quantization gives cost and throughput benefits with small quality delta for most prompts.
[07:59] Rajiv: That aligns with what we need to present to procurement. We'll need the SOC2 + KMS doc and the final side-by-side demo.
[08:07] Jordan: Action items and next steps we already captured. We'll aim to share the updated sheet by tomorrow and the re-run by Friday.
[08:18] Ana: Thanks everyone. One small transcribe note, some names might be garbled in the automated notes.
[08:25] Jordan: Yep noted. Anything else? No? Cool thanks, we'll follow up in email.
[08:33] Samantha: Thanks all.

End of transcript.

Notes on transcription quality: medium - occasional mislabels and minor word swaps (eg. "kv cache" sometimes transcribed as "key v cache").
